A language model $p$ is a distribution over $\Sigma^*$ where $\Sigma$ is an alphabet. The elements of $\Sigma$ are tokens. A string $\boldsymbol{w} = w_1 \cdots w_N$ of length $N$ is a finite sequence of tokens $w_n \in \Sigma$ . Most modern LLMs are defined in an autoregressive manner, i.e.,

$$
p (\boldsymbol {w}) = p \left(\operatorname {E O S} \mid \boldsymbol {w}\right) \prod_ {n = 1} ^ {N} p \left(w _ {n} \mid \boldsymbol {w} _ {<   n}\right), \tag {1}
$$

and each local conditional distribution $p(\cdot \mid \boldsymbol{w}_{< n})$ is defined over $\overline{\Sigma} \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=} \Sigma \cup \{\mathrm{EOS}\}$ . We denote $\boldsymbol{w}_{< n} \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=} w_{1} \cdots w_{n-1}$ and $\boldsymbol{w}_{< 1} \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=} \varepsilon$ . Note that not all models defined as in (1) are distributions over $\Sigma^{*}$ . However, in the context of our paper, we assume $p$ is.

Tasks. As shown in Tab. 3 (App. C.1), we select 3 commonly used text classification datasets for ICL: Customer Reviews (CR; Hu and Liu, 2004), Stanford Sentiment Treebank with binary sentiments (SST-2; Socher et al., 2013), and AG News (Zhang et al., 2015); see App. D for the license details.

Experimental Setup. Each text classification dataset contains a set of pairs $\{(\pmb{x}^{(\ell)},y^{(\ell)})\}_{\ell = 1}^{L}$ where $\pmb{x}^{(\ell)}\in \Sigma^{*}$ is an input string and $y^{(\ell)}\in Y$ is $\pmb{x}^{(\ell)}$ 's classification label drawn from $Y$ , a finite, task-dependent label set. To encode a classification problem as ICL, we map each element of $Y$ to a string in $\Sigma^{*}$ by means of a function $o\colon Y\to \Sigma^{*}$ . Additionally, we convert the input $\pmb{x}$ into a prompt $\pmb{p}$ through a templating function $t\colon \Sigma^{*}\to \Sigma^{*}$ . The exact templating function we use for each dataset is listed in Tab. 3. Then, we construct a delimiter-separated demonstration of size $L$ : $\pmb {d} = t(\pmb{x}^{(1)})o(y^{(1)})\sharp \dots \sharp t(\pmb{x}^{(L)})o(y^{(L)})$ . To perform classification on a test prompt $t(\pmb {x})$ , we select the highest-probability class as follows

$$
y ^ {\star} = \underset {\widetilde {y} \in Y} {\operatorname {a r g m a x}} p \left(o (\widetilde {y}) \mid d _ {\mathfrak {q}} t (x)\right). \tag {6}
$$

Settings. We consider three settings: (1) Chance: random guessing uniformly across different classes; (2) Vanilla ICL: the standard ICL setting; (3) $\tau_{\mathrm{RA}}$ -ICL: The responses $\pmb{r}$ in the

demonstrations are replaced by $g(\boldsymbol{r})$ . The prompts $\boldsymbol{p}$ are left unchanged.

Implementation Details. We conduct experiments on a publicly available LLM: LLaMA2 (Touvron et al., 2023) with three sizes: 7B, 13B, and 70B. Each experiment is repeated 20 times with different random seeds and the average F1-Macro score is reported. In each experiment, we construct a distinct test set consisting of 256 prompt-response pairs, and for each element of this test set, we sample $L$ prompt-response pairs from the training set, which serve as its demonstration.

Our experimental setup follows $\S 3.1$ . However, we introduce two more settings in addition to the ones we consider in $\S 3.1$ :

- $\tau_{\mathbf{PA}}$ -ICL: As defined in (7), the prompts $p$ (including the template tokens such as "Review" and "Sentiment") in the demonstrations are replaced with $h(p)$ . The responses $r$ are left unchanged.   
- $\tau_{\mathrm{PA}}$ -LR: To make sure a PA task $\tau_{\mathrm{PA}}$ is learnable from a demonstration, we fit a logistic regression (LR) model as a baseline. Because a variable-length string cannot be easily fed into a logistic regressor, we first tokenize a string using the LLaMA2 tokenizer and then convert it into bag-of-words (BoW) representations. The classifier is then trained using a BoW representation of exactly the same $L$ prompt-response pairs as used in a demonstration of $\tau_{\mathrm{PA}}$ -ICL. We use this baseline to gauge the performance of a model with minimum learning ability.

Tasks. In addition to CR, SST-2, and AG News, we also consider DBpedia (Zhang et al., 2015), which has many more classes (Tab. 3).

Experimental Setup. We consider the task $\tau_{g}$ induced by the string-to-string function $g$ , as introduced in § 3. Given string-label pairs $\{(\pmb{x}^{(\ell)}, y^{(\ell)})\}_{\ell=1}^{L}$ , we construct a demonstration for task $\tau_{g}$ as follows: $o(y^{(1)}) g(o(y^{(1)})) \vdash \dots \vdash o(y^{(L)}) g(o(y^{(L)}))$ , i.e., $\pmb{p}_{\ell} = o(y^{(\ell)})$ and $\pmb{r}_{\ell} = g(o(y^{(\ell)}))$ . In this

formulation, both prompts and responses consist of a single token, i.e., $\pmb{p}, \pmb{r} \in \Sigma$ . We denote the set of distinct responses as $R \subset \Sigma$ .

The single-token construction allows us to model the task using linear regression. The embedding layer $(0^{\mathrm{th}}$ layer) of an LLM is a matrix $\mathbf{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\Sigma| \times D}$ , where $D$ is the dimensionality of embeddings. We retrieve the row vector $\mathbf{p}_{\ell} \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=} \mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{p}_{\ell},:} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times D}$ for each prompt $\mathbf{p}_{\ell}$ , where $\mathbf{E}_{\mathbf{p}_{\ell},:}$ denotes the row vector in $\mathbf{E}$ that corresponds to the token $\mathbf{p}_{\ell}$ . We vertically stack the row vectors to create the embedding matrix $\mathbf{P} \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times D}$ of the prompts in the demonstration. Also, let $\mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times D}$ be a similarly constructed embedding matrix of the responses, i.e., each response $\mathbf{r}_{\ell}$ is embedded as a row vector $\mathbf{r}_{\ell} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times D}$ . Additionally, for a test prompt-response pair $\langle \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{r} \rangle = \langle o(y), g(o(y)) \rangle$ , we embed the prompt $\mathbf{p}$ as a row vector $\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times D}$ . Thus, learning $\tau_{g}$ is reduced to performing a multiple linear regression, i.e., learning a parameter matrix $\mathbf{W}^{\star} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}$ that minimizes the following (nonstrictly) convex objective

$$
\mathbf {W} ^ {\star} \in \underset {\mathbf {W}} {\operatorname {a r g m a x}} \left\| \mathbf {R} - \mathbf {P W} \right\| ^ {2}. \tag {8}
$$

Moreover, the data are constructed such that the test prompt-response pair $\langle \pmb{p},\pmb{r}\rangle$ has appeared at least once in $\{\langle \pmb{p}_{\ell},\pmb{r}_{\ell}\rangle \}_{\ell = 1}^{L}$ , so the task does not require generalization at all.

Settings. We compare the following two settings:

- $\tau_{g}$ -ICL: We construct a demonstration $d = p_1r_1\vdash \dots \vdash p_Lr_L$ and perform classification as follows:

$$
\boldsymbol {r} ^ {\star} = \underset {\widetilde {\boldsymbol {r}} \in R} {\operatorname {a r g m a x}} p (\widetilde {\boldsymbol {r}} \mid \boldsymbol {d} \sharp \boldsymbol {p}). \tag {9}
$$

The classification is correct if $r^{\star} = r$ .

- $\tau_{g}$ -Linear: We train a linear regression with gradient descent. At inference time, we use a minimizer $\mathbf{W}^{\star}$ to compute the predicted embedding

The dashed horizontal line represents the performance of random guessing (i.e., Chance). The Pearson correlation coefficients $\gamma_{\mathrm{p}}$ and Spearman correlation coefficients $\gamma_{\mathrm{s}}$ are also reported. vector $\mathbf{r}^{\star}$ for $\pmb{r}$ as follows

$$
\mathbf {r} ^ {\star} = \mathbf {p} \mathbf {W} ^ {\star} \in \mathbb {R} ^ {1 \times D}. \tag {10}
$$

In order to evaluate its performance against ICL, we utilize the transposed embedding layer $\mathbf{E}^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times |\Sigma|}$ to project $\mathbf{r}^{\star}$ into $\mathbb{R}^{1 \times |\Sigma|}$ and perform classification as follows:

$$
\boldsymbol {r} ^ {\star} = \underset {\widetilde {\boldsymbol {r}} \in R} {\operatorname {a r g m a x}} \left(\mathbf {r} ^ {\star} \mathbf {E} ^ {\top}\right) _ {\widetilde {\boldsymbol {r}}}. \tag {11}
$$

where $(\mathbf{r}^{\star}\mathbf{E}^{\top})_{\widetilde{\boldsymbol{r}}}$ denotes the entry of the vector $(\mathbf{r}^{\star}\mathbf{E}^{\top})$ that corresponds to the token $\widetilde{r}$ . We judge classification correct if $r^{\star} = r$ . Note that the embedding layer $\mathbf{E}$ is taken directly from the LLM and not trained with the linear model.

Implementation Details. For all the following experiments in § 4.2 and § 5, we experiment on the largest model (LLaMA2-70B) and set the demonstration length $L = 32$ . We randomly sample 500 functions $g$ for $\tau_g$ . Each mapping $g$ is constructed by randomly selecting a token from $\Sigma$ as the image $g(o(y))$ of a $o(y)$ . We train $\tau_g$ -Linear with also 32 examples for 80 epochs which corresponds to the 80 layers of LLaMA2-70B. We choose a learning rate of 1000, which we find yields the best performance. The correlation between the F1-Macro scores of $\tau_g$ -ICL and $\tau_g$ -Linear is computed.

The experimental setup of $\tau_{\mathrm{RA}}$ -ICL and $\tau_{g}$ -ICL follow that of $\S 3.1$ and $\S 4.2$ , respectively. The correlation between the F1-Macro scores of $\tau_{\mathrm{RA}}$ -ICL and $\tau_{g}$ -ICL is computed.

We consider three types of natural functions: (1) synonym: Each prompt $o(y)$ is mapped to one of its synonyms, (2) antonym: Each prompt $o(y)$ is mapped to one of its antonyms, and (3) keyword: Each prompt $o(y)$ is mapped to a keyword in its genre. Synonyms and antonyms are selected using PyMultiDictionary library. Keywords are obtained for each genre by querying GPT-4 (OpenAI, 2023). In contrast to random, we cannot create a large number of natural functions as easily. Therefore, we manually choose a candidate set of 10 possible synonyms (resp. antonyms and keywords) for each prompt. Thus, we can create a natural function by sampling a synonym (resp. antonym and keyword), from the candidate sets for every input. We create 500 such functions.

The powers of the synonym functions are created the same way as in § 5.2.1. Because the candidate sets of synonyms are small (of size 10), to demonstrate how it is possible to create seemingly arbitrary functions, we adversarially sample functions such that for every $\pmb{p}$ , $g_{\mathrm{syn}}^m(\pmb{p}) \in S^m(\pmb{p}) \setminus S^{m-1}(\pmb{p})$ , where $S^m(\pmb{p})$ denotes the set of all the $m^{\mathrm{th}}$ order synonyms of $\pmb{p}$ , i.e., we only keep those that are not synonyms of lower orders. As an example of this strategy, we may have the following mapping: "company" is synonymous with "firm", which is synonymous with "association" (as a noun) and "adamant" (as an adjective). Thus, we would map "adamant" to "company", a seemingly unrelated word.

In order to evaluate its performance against ICL, we utilize the transposed embedding layer $\mathbf{E}^{\top} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times |\Sigma|}$ to project $\mathbf{r}^{\star}$ into $\mathbb{R}^{1 \times |\Sigma|}$ and perform classification as follows:

We judge classification correct if $r^{\star} = r$ . Note that the embedding layer $\mathbf{E}$ is taken directly from the LLM and not trained with the linear model.

Implementation Details. For all the following experiments in § 4.2 and § 5, we experiment on the largest model (LLaMA2-70B) and set the demonstration length $L = 32$ . We randomly sample 500 functions $g$ for $\tau_g$ . Each mapping $g$ is constructed by randomly selecting a token from $\Sigma$ as the image $g(o(y))$ of a $o(y)$ . We train $\tau_g$ -Linear with also 32 examples for 80 epochs which corresponds to the 80 layers of LLaMA2-70B. We choose a learning rate of 1000, which we find yields the best performance. The correlation between the F1-Macro scores of $\tau_g$ -ICL and $\tau_g$ -Linear is computed.

The experimental setup of $\tau_{\mathrm{RA}}$ -ICL and $\tau_{g}$ -ICL follow that of $\S 3.1$ and $\S 4.2$ , respectively. The correlation between the F1-Macro scores of $\tau_{\mathrm{RA}}$ -ICL and $\tau_{g}$ -ICL is computed.

We consider three types of natural functions: (1) synonym: Each prompt $o(y)$ is mapped to one of its synonyms, (2) antonym: Each prompt $o(y)$ is mapped to one of its antonyms, and (3) keyword: Each prompt $o(y)$ is mapped to a keyword in its genre. Synonyms and antonyms are selected using PyMultiDictionary library. Keywords are obtained for each genre by querying GPT-4 (OpenAI, 2023). In contrast to random, we cannot create a large number of natural functions as easily. Therefore, we manually choose a candidate set of 10 possible synonyms (resp. antonyms and keywords) for each prompt. Thus, we can create a natural function by sampling a synonym (resp. antonym and keyword), from the candidate sets for every input. We create 500 such functions.

The powers of the synonym functions are created the same way as in § 5.2.1. Because the candidate sets of synonyms are small (of size 10), to demonstrate how it is possible to create seemingly arbitrary functions, we adversarially sample functions such that for every $\pmb{p}$ , $g_{\mathrm{syn}}^m(\pmb{p}) \in S^m(\pmb{p}) \setminus S^{m-1}(\pmb{p})$ , where $S^m(\pmb{p})$ denotes the set of all the $m^{\mathrm{th}}$ order synonyms of $\pmb{p}$ , i.e., we only keep those that are not synonyms of lower orders. As an example of this strategy, we may have the following mapping: "company" is synonymous with "firm", which is synonymous with "association" (as a noun) and "adamant" (as an adjective). Thus, we would map "adamant" to "company", a seemingly unrelated word.
